prompt: A delay speaker stands 40 m in front of the main speakers. You set its delay (about 117 ms, ignoring latency) so that both arrivals line up for a reference listener 10 m behind the delay speaker, on the straight line from the main speakers through the delay speaker. Which other listener also hears the two arrivals lined up?

options.text: A listener halfway between the main speakers and the delay speaker
options.explanation: There the main path is short and the delay path long, so the path difference is much less than 40 m. The delayed speaker arrives late and can sound like an echo.

options.text: Everyone in the venue: the delay corrects all positions
options.explanation: A single delay matches a single path difference. It only lines up where the difference equals the one you designed for.

options.text: A listener 20 m further back on the same line
options.explanation: Correct. Moving straight back along that line adds the same distance to both paths, so their difference, and the alignment, stay the same.
Positions along the same line beyond the delay speaker share the same path difference, so they are aligned too.

workedExample:
1. The delay compensates the extra travel time of the main speakers' sound: the path difference divided by the speed of sound.
2. At the reference listener, the main path is 40 m longer than the delay path.
3. 20 m further back on the same line, both paths grow by 20 m, so the main path is still 40 m longer: still aligned.
4. Between the main speakers and the delay speaker, the main path is short and the delay path long, so the delay speaker's sound arrives late.

That is why delay speakers face away from the stage and cover the area behind them. Any extra precedence offset is a design choice to verify by measuring and listening.

link.title: Auditory pathways and localisation — David Heeger, NYU

prompt: Which statements about PA system components are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Subwoofer arrays can be arranged (for example cardioid or end-fire) to reduce low-frequency energy on stage
options.explanation: Correct. Several subs with suitable spacing and delay steer bass.

options.text: Monitor wedges are normally fed from the main L/R mix
options.explanation: Monitors get separate pre-fader aux mixes tailored to each performer.

options.text: Front fills cover the front rows, who are below the main speakers' coverage
Line arrays control vertical coverage and lose level more slowly with distance over part of their range
options.explanation: Correct. Over part of their range they behave more like a line than a point source.

workedExample:
Typical PA components:

- main speakers (point source or line array) for the audience.
- Subs for below ~80–120 Hz, sometimes in steerable arrays.
- Front fills for the front rows.
- Delays for the back of large venues.
- Monitors (wedges, side fills, IEMs) from aux mixes.
